title: Indian Investors Rush Into Nvidia, SpaceX and Apple as Apps Open US Stock Access
excerpt: Groww has opened US trading to all customers, Zerodha is in beta and Angel One is next, as a falling Nifty and a weak rupee push India's retail investors toward Wall Street.
body:
• India's biggest brokerages are opening US stock trading to millions of retail customers: Groww has rolled it out to all users, Zerodha is in beta with a launch in weeks, and Angel One is preparing to follow.
  • The push comes as the Nifty 50 has fallen nearly 13% this year while the S&P 500 has gained over 12%, and foreign investors have pulled a record $32.5 billion from Indian equities.
  • Early Groww users are buying Nvidia, SpaceX and Apple most; the platform offers 10,000+ US stocks and ETFs with fractional shares at 0.1% brokerage.
  • Resident Indians sent $321 million overseas for stock and bond investing in August alone, up 111% year on year — investments are now 11.7% of all outward remittances, double the share of a year ago.

Indian investment platforms are expanding access to US stocks as local markets underperform, with Nvidia, SpaceX and Apple among the most popular picks among early users of Groww's new trading feature, according to CNBC reporting summarized by KuCoin News. Until now, direct access to US markets was largely the preserve of wealthier Indians investing through global banks and wealth managers.

What the platforms are offering

Groww, which accounts for more than 29% of India's 46 million active brokerage investors, has rolled the feature out to all customers after a phased launch to select users about three weeks earlier. It offers access to more than 10,000 US-listed stocks and exchange-traded funds, along with fractional investing, which lets users buy a portion of a share instead of a whole one. Groww charges brokerage of 0.1% of the transaction value, the Hindu BusinessLine reported. Zerodha, with a 15% share of active clients, is beta testing US stock access and plans to launch within weeks; Angel One, with 6.7 million active retail clients, is also reportedly planning to add the service.

"There has always been underlying demand in India to invest in global companies."

— Somnath Mukherjee, Vice President of Corporate Development, Zerodha

"As Indian investors mature, their financial aspirations naturally expand beyond domestic markets. Many users today follow global companies, consume global products, and work in globally connected industries," Groww co-founder and COO Harsh Jain said. Among the popular stocks on the platform are Nvidia, SpaceX, Apple, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, Micron, Tesla and Netflix, with semiconductors and artificial intelligence, space technology and big technology the popular themes.

Why now: a weak home market and a weak rupee

The timing is driven by divergence. India's benchmark Nifty 50 has fallen nearly 13% since the start of the year, while the S&P 500 has risen over 12%. NSDL data shows foreign investors have withdrawn a record $32.5 billion in direct equity investments since January. Zerodha's Mukherjee told CNBC that India's underperforming market, the lack of domestic AI leaders and rupee depreciation — which prompts investors to "allocate a portion of their portfolios into another currency" — are driving demand. Reserve Bank of India data shows resident Indians sent over $321 million overseas for stock and bond investments in August, a 111% increase from a year earlier, and $2.6 billion across the financial year ended March 2026. Investments now account for 11.7% of total overseas remittances, up from 5.8% a year ago.

The currency question regulators will watch

The shift has a macro edge. Tanvi Kanchan of Anand Rathi Shares & Stock Brokers noted that while retail outflows are still small against India's foreign exchange reserves, they tend to rise precisely when the rupee weakens and US markets strengthen, "amplifying pressure at the worst possible time." Kotak Mahindra Asset Management Singapore's Nitin Jain warned that as participation grows, Indian regulators may "reconsider" how widely US market access is allowed. For now, though, the direction is one-way: the apps that onboarded a generation of Indian investors into domestic equities are turning the same one-tap experience toward Wall Street — and the first thing those investors are buying is the AI trade they cannot get at home.
